title: Bendōwa 3 - Transmission of the Dharma
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: In a Soto Zen dharma talk, Nomon Tim Burnett reflects on the importance of lineage in understanding Buddhism's true teachings, acknowledging that while patriarchal language may be present, it is still valuable and worthy of appreciation. They emphasize that true understanding comes from direct experience and practice, rather than just intellectual knowledge or reading about it. Nomon encourages listeners to let go of conceptual thinking and instead directly experience reality, allowing awakening to happen naturally through curiosity and attention.
topics: Dogen's writings (specifically referenced in the talk but not explicitly named)

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Well, I just want to take a moment to say thank you.
I thank everybody who was involved in our big ceremony on Sunday, and the weeks and months and decades of preparation that went into it.
It's quite something, beautiful and humbling.
This is going to sound kind of dumb, but one of the things I was really grateful for was that I remembered to take my watch off.
You're not really supposed to be in the zendo with a watch, particularly not for a big important ceremony.

When we were doing the week of ceremonies with Norman for dharma transmission, I had my watch on for the most important one, denbo, when you receive the special gear and the blessing and all kinds of stuff, and then Norman's like, "Hey, you shouldn't really be wearing your watch."
Stuff sticks with you, you know?
So anyway, it's funny what the mind can come up with to worry about or not worry about.
But really I'm just grateful, it's so moving.
It wasn't about me per se.
It was about all of us together and what we could create together.
We could bring forward love and connection, and drop all of our silly stuff for a little while.
It came back though, I bet, huh?
Not yet.
Oh good, good, not yet.
So let's continue exploring Dogen's writing Bendowa, the wholehearted way, one might translate it, or endeavors on the way.
If you're just joining us, this is Eihei Dogen, 12th century Japanese Zen priest, credited as the first ancestor.
It does fit the historical facts pretty well to say that about him.
He went to China as a young man, one of the first, but not the first, Japanese monks to go to China and see what the Chinese Zen, Chan, masters were doing.
He studied with the teacher there and brought back a deep feeling for practice and a deep feeling for life really.

In the last installment, remember, he started out by explaining the essence of what he feels is important about practice, the sense of just being deeply in your life, and then he was bemoaning that maybe nobody was going to understand this, which is a traditional thing to worry about.
The Buddha worried about that too.
In the main story of the Buddha's enlightenment, after his awakening, he was worried nobody would get it.
He was just going to hang out in bliss for the rest of the aeon, but then one of the gods appeared and talked him into teaching.
And he thought, man, maybe somebody does have not too much dust in their eyes.
Maybe somebody would understand it.
So Dogen is basically riffing off the Buddha, and he says something like that: there's got to be some who could hear this way of teaching, this way of practice.
Where we ended was he said, okay, since you might have trouble tracking me down, I'm going to write it down for you.
He writes:
*At the great Zen monasteries in China, I saw with my own eyes and have learned the profound teachings of the masters that I have succeeded to follow and transmit.
I want such seekers of the way to know the right Dharma.
Here are the true essentials.*
Okay, so now he's going to tell us the true essentials.
Well, what does he start out with?
Lineage.
He starts out with lineage.
He writes:
*At an assembly on Vulture Peak, the great teacher Shakyamuni Buddha imparted to Mahakasyapa the Dharma that was subsequently transmitted from patriarch to patriarch down to Bodhidharma.
Bodhidharma traveled to China and conveyed the Dharma to Weika, marking the initial transmission of the Bodhidharma to eastern lands.
It then made its way in direct personal transmission to the sixth patriarch, Ta-Chin Weika*
or I mean Huineng.
Ta-Chin is one of his names, Huineng.
*And by that time the genuine Bodhidharma had beyond doubt spread extensively in China.
It appeared there with its essence unaffected by any ramifying doctrinal accretions.*
The good stuff.
We found the good stuff finally.
*The sixth patriarch had two superior disciples, Huai-Zhang of Nanyue and Xing-Xiu of Qiang-Yuan.
As possessors and transmitters of the Buddha seal, they were masters for men and devas alike.
Their two schools spread and branched into five houses, the Fa-Yan, Kui-Yang, Sao-Tung, Yun-Men, and Lin-Chi schools.
Present in the Great Song China, the Lin-Chi house alone is found throughout the country.
Among those five houses there are differences to be found, but they all equally hold the one Buddha mind seal.*
I'm feeling a little called to apologize for the male language, but that's the way they translated it, and I assume it's reasonably accurate to what he wrote.
As we'll see later though, Dogen even from the beginning understood strongly that women could practice equally to men.
But it does have patriarchal language because this traditional lineage, which is a wonderful mythology in its way, is a male lineage, all men.
Maybe later on we'll return to some of the wonderful stories of the many women teachers who really were part of this equally.

But the beauty and the downfall of the Zen lineage conception is that it's from one teacher to one student to one teacher to one student, like in a line, and they just riffed on the power of that idea, this line going back to Buddha.
So when you do any of the ordination ceremonies, even the Jukai ceremony, which is a sort of lay ordination, you receive a document with the line, which is very powerful and also a little flawed.
So our question is: how do we work with what we've received in the best way?
In the first lecture on Bendowa I mentioned that there maybe are three different kinds of truth that we could play with when we study these traditional texts.
The first is the historical truth of it.
In fact, to make this beautiful line work they had to fudge it at a few points in history, because actually there was nobody there, so they had to put somebody else in.
Because somebody studied with somebody else, it's not really a straight line in essence, right?
You study with many teachers.
So there's a historical truth, which is true in some ways, and in other ways it's a little bit made up.

Then secondly there's a devotional truth, which is really worth embracing even with the sexist flaw here: that these were wonderful, powerful teachers, that it really happened the way Dogen expresses, and that we can feel their presence here in the room with us now.
It's a wondrous thing that for thousands of years these deep practitioners of the way kept the flame alive and passed it on to us.
So we have historical truth, devotional truth, and then the third truth is practical truth, practice truth.
How do we practice with this?
Well, it's a holding of different things, right?
Holding the beauty and the flaws together with appreciation, and doing what we can to correct the flaws.
So we have a wonderful book that our dear colleague Florence Caplow and Susan Moon put together, collecting the women's stories, women's and teacher's stories, which should be in our library, I hope.
And then also we appreciate and we bow down and we revere the traditional lineage too, because it's also wonderful.
In the ceremony on Sunday, if you weren't there, I had to make a bunch of statements, and a couple of them were statements of lineage.
Here's part of my statement for my teacher, and I was making little offerings before each statement:
*This offering is for my root heart teacher, Soketsu Rincho Norman Fischer.
It's now been 30 years since a 21-year-old new Zen student and a 41-year-old new Zen teacher first sat together to explore this way of practice.
In every one of those 30 years, I have been deeply supported by this good fortune to practice and study with you.
My gratitude can't be expressed, but the ceremony says I need to try.*
I learned that from him too, slipping little jokes in like that.
Lighten things up.
And I go on:
*Thank you for sharing with me your deep faith in people's natural ability to heal and grow.
Thank you for sharing with me your deep faith in our Zen way of practice and our family style, that it's enough to practice together, steadily, devotedly, over time, that this is enough.*
So that's really what Dogen felt.
He learned this feeling from his teacher in China, which none of the teachers in Japan quite could express in a way that he could appreciate.
And so he came back to China to try to bring this feeling forward.
He recognized that you can write about it, you can talk about it, and he wrote extensively and spoke extensively about it, but it comes down to a feeling that is human.
Let's go on here.
In the next paragraph he's going to talk about how it went down in China.
*Scriptural writings were transmitted to China from the Western land during the latter Han dynasty.
These scriptures spread over the empire, but even in China, no determination was reached about which of the various teachings was superior.
Following the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West, these entangling complications were cut away at their source.
And the one Buddha Dharma, free from all impurity, began to spread.
We must pray that this will happen in our country as well.*
So in there you get a picture.
He's 32, I think, when he writes this.
And there's Buddhism and all kinds of spirituality and a very dynamic and topsy-turvy socio-political situation happening in China, I mean in Japan, kind of like here now.
Things are kind of going to hell.
There's a lot of authoritarianism actually in Tokugawa, Japan, like a lot.
And he's not really sure what's going to happen.
How's this going to go?
So we must pray that this will take place, that this will root itself in our country.
And let's pray for that here too.
This understanding, this sense of presence and kindness and compassion, this way of being that's beyond our concepts, is essential and important to human beings.
So let's pray that that takes root in our culture and our political discourse too.
It's funny too, because our way of practice is pretty subtle, and there's a depth to it.
But when you say it's subtle and deep, that's way too grandiose.
That's not right.
It's also ordinary.
But the essence of this isn't really quite graspable by the usual mind that acquires skills and information.
And in many ways, this way of practice literally doesn't make much sense.
For a while, Norman used to go around saying, "The great thing about zazen, the great thing about Zen meditation, is that it's useless.
That's what's good about it."
Some other forms of practice appear to be more concrete, with techniques and results and things you can expect, more graspable, at least on the surface.
Although I think ultimately all human endeavor has the same kind of depth that we're interested in.
But our way just doesn't give you a whole lot.
It doesn't give you handles exactly.
It just encourages you to drop into it, to settle in it, to sit in it, to rest in it, and have a lot of faith in it.
And that would never work if you didn't have the company of people who had already been doing that for many years.

Because you feel something, you connect to something in relationship to them, whether it's something you think you perceive in them, or something that their presence helps you feel in yourself, or just something in the air, I don't know.
When I first went to the practice places as a young man, I had some feeling, like there's something to this.
I didn't know quite what it was, but there's something to it.
And progress, such as it is, and how could there exactly be progress in this?
But if there was progress, it would be slow.
Suzuki Roshi said this:
*After you practice for a while, you will realize that it's not possible to make rapid extraordinary progress.
And even though you try very hard, the progress you make is little by little.
It's not like going into the shower, which you know you'll get wet right away.
It's more like a fog.
You don't know you're getting wet.
But as you keep walking, you get wet little by little.
So if your mind has ideas of progress, you may say, oh, the pace is terrible.
But actually, it's not.
When you get wet in a fog, it's very difficult to dry yourself.*
That's the good thing.
You can't get dry either.
*So there's no need to worry about progress.*
So that's what we are trying to do or not do here.
But it's hard for us to have much confidence in a subtle, ungraspable process that you can't even feel.
You can't exactly know in that way of knowing.
So Dogen talks about the lineage, and he starts by referencing the classic first lineage story, which he barely mentions here.
He says the great teacher Shakyamuni Buddha imparted to Mahakasyapa the Dharma.
And there's a wonderful story about this.
At one time, the Buddha sat down to give the Dharma talk, the daily talk, and he didn't say anything.
He sat there quietly for a while, and then he held up a flower.
Various translations say he held up a flower and winked, or blinked, or had a twinkle in his eye.
Reverend Norman says a twinkle in his eye held up the flower.
It wasn't just holding up the flower.
There was something with his eye going on too.
And then nobody knew what to make of this, except one student saw this flower, saw the Buddha's kind eye, and broke out into a big smile.
They don't use this language, of course, but it's basically like a shit-eating grin.
And the World-Honored One, the Buddha, looked at Mahakasyapa and saw this had happened and said, "I have the eye of the true Dharma, the wondrous heart of Nirvana.
This I transmit to Mahakasyapa."
So there's the beginning, right?
One to one, teacher to student.
Now, Mahakasyapa was indeed one of the principal disciples of Buddha.
The usual count is 16 principal disciples, and I think there's reasonable historic evidence that these people all existed.
But there's nothing outside these Zen stories to suggest that the Buddha had the idea that one of them would be foremost or most central.
Different students were foremost in different aspects of practice, and Mahakasyapa was foremost in ascetic practice.
That's interesting because of the whole story of the Buddha, in which he did serious hardcore ascetic practice for many years, just about killed himself, and then gave it up.
So it's interesting that the Zen tradition picked his disciple foremost in ascetic practice to be the first great Zen ancestor.
They could have picked one of the ones who was foremost in wisdom or foremost in ethics, but they picked him.
So we get our hardcore sort of reputation from early on.
Then, as we read, Dogen goes on to talk about a process of cultural change.
The teachings come into the culture and people aren't sure what to make of them, and then teachers emerge and it becomes more clear.
In this case the teacher who emerged is Bodhidharma, and it's dicey whether he really existed.
He may have been an amalgamation of different Indian monks who came to China.
He may have been myth, or he may have existed just the way it says.
So then he goes on:

*It is said that all the patriarchs and Buddhas who have maintained the Buddhadharma have without question considered practice based on proper sitting in Jijuyu Samadhi as the right path that led to their enlightenment.
All those who have gained enlightenment in India and China have followed this way of practice.
It is a matter of rightly transmitting the wonderful means in personal encounter from master to disciple, and on the disciples sustaining the true essence thus received.*
So this is like going back to the beginning, but now he's folding it into lineage.
If you remember way back in the beginning, he talked about this Jijuyu Samadhi, this self-fulfilling, joyful essence of being alive, of practice.
But at the beginning he said it can only be passed from a Buddha to a Buddha.
Remember that?
Now he says it can be passed from teacher to disciple, from master to disciple.
And it's the obligation and the responsibility and the joy of the disciple to sustain it.
To sustain it.
So after the [unclear: "back to my"] Dharma transmission ceremony with Norman, when was that? 2011, I think.
After going through this whole week of lots of ceremonies, and it was not exhausting or anything.
We got up really early every morning and there was lots of stuff to do, but we had downtime.
It was a sweet week.
I wish I had been better at napping at the time, because we did stuff really early and then we did stuff at midnight.
There were these long breaks in the day, and we created different documents.
There's a lot to it, but it wasn't that difficult, though it was intense.
Anyway, we completed all that.
The final thing was done.
We took the pictures and all this.
Then I wandered down the hill, and just a couple of streets down from where Norman lives was another early teacher of mine, a priest named Lee de Barros.
Lee de Barros very kindly made me lunch and congratulated me and sat me down.
And the first thing he wanted to say was exactly what Dogen was saying here.
He said, "Okay, now that you have completed this transmission, you need to find a disciple."
I'm like, "Oh man, can I just have lunch first?"
He's a very sweet, casual guy.
I was really surprised that he even gave me this very traditional teaching, like, "Okay, Tim, don't mess around."
I appreciate that.
It was kind of him.
It was a kindness.
So that's what Dogen says too.
Now, back to this idea of Jijuyu Samadhi.
Is it important that we parse out and understand exactly what that word means?
I'm not sure, and interestingly, he doesn't.

You would think, in our logical, linear way of thinking about things, that since in his first breakout essay he says this is the most important thing, Jijuyu Samadhi, he would have gone on to write and talk about this the rest of his career.
But not so much.
He only mentions it in his writing, I think, two more times ever, out of thousands and thousands of words.
And it was not a very commonly used term in China before him either.
So that's a little bit interesting and puzzling.
Our colleagues seem to think that it's just something he turned over for a time and found helpful, found interesting, and it seemed like a good expression of what he was trying to understand.
Then he found other ways.
There are many, many ways to express it, which is beautiful in its way too, that there's no one way to express this.
That was a central teaching of Suzuki Roshi as well.
Somebody asked Suzuki Roshi, I forget exactly the question, but something like, "What's the most essential quality of Zen Buddhism?
What's the most important teaching of Zen?"
And he said two words, "Not always so."
Oops, three words in English: "Not always so."
So many, many expressions, no one expression.
So we can parse out and study Jijuyu Samadhi, that's good, but it's not like if we don't figure this out we're never going to get it.
Another failure in my Zen career!
But essentially it means we can allow awakening to take care of itself and to take care of us.
We need to show up, we need to practice, we need to be here, we need to be really curious about our assumptions about ourselves in this universe, because they're probably not quite right.
And we need to steep and marinate and immerse ourselves in this steadily for years.
But we don't have to fix it, we don't have to do it, we don't have to make it happen.
This understanding is self-fulfilling, self-powered.
It takes care of itself.
That kind of self, not our kind of self.
And the really interesting thing, with Zen's dour reputation, is that two of these characters put together, I understand, have a quality of joy and engagement and delight.
So it's a delightful thing too.
There's another wonderful book on this text called *The Wholehearted Way*.
It's a translation by two other authors, some of whom we know: Taigen Leighton and Shohaku Okumura.
And [unclear: "Andrea Sons"] studies with Shohaku Roshi, and they are translating Shohaku's teacher, Uchiyama Roshi.
So here's a little bit from Uchiyama Roshi commenting on this passage of the text.
That's in our library, you can get it, called *The Wholehearted Way*.
When Dogen circles back around to Jijuyu Zanmai, Jijuyu Samadhi again, Uchiyama comments:
*We should not listen to the Buddha Dharma in a light way.
We have to listen to the Buddha Dharma in a way such that the Dharma permeates to the core of our mind and becomes our bone and marrow, so that we won't forget it no matter what happens to us.
This is the crucial point of Bendowa.
Unless we grasp this, we will never be able to understand Bendowa as Buddha Dharma.
Although we always think that we are really living, as a matter of fact we are not living out the reality of life.
It is essential to become aware of this fact.
Well then, in what way are we living?
We're not really living in the reality of life.
So how are we living?
In a word, each and every one of us lives by treating abstract concepts as real.*
So this is taking things a bit further than last week.
So this is taking things a bit further than when I was talking about some forms of practice.
It's a little more tangible, maybe a little more sensible.
We don't really have much to hold on to.
Uchiyama Roshi is saying, well, actually, no concept is something you can hold on to, and your concepts are all a little bit off anyway.
So stop living through concepts.
And cognitive science agrees with this, that there's a quality of mind they call reification, the mind's ability to make things that are just thoughts, just concepts, seem to be real.
So Uchiyama is calling out this quality of mind, that we believe in the reification of the mind.
Here's a classic thought experiment to point out reification.
Try this out.
Imagine a strawberry.
Really imagine this: a luscious, red, juicy-looking strawberry.
Imagine you're holding it in your hand, you can smell it, maybe it's a beautiful sunny day too.
Let's go all out, and you're about to bite into it.
Does your body respond to that?
Yeah.
It's just a thought.
There's no strawberry, but the salivation starts.
You're like, "Oh good, it's going to be so good."
But here's the thing.
When we eat a real strawberry, that's what we're doing.
We're not really eating the real strawberry, usually.
We're eating our concept of a strawberry, and the mind is filling in all the details for us, triggered by various sensations and all this, but not fully really tasting the strawberry.
Practice can help us to actually taste the real strawberry, to actually see the real person, to actually feel the real breeze, to go beyond concepts.
And when you directly experience the real reality, it's so heartbreaking and heart-stopping.
It's beautiful, and every one of us has these experiences.
It's not an artifact of being a clever Zen student.
Maybe it's been a while, maybe you need to bring your memory back to childhood or something like that.
But maybe it is true that children are not so hampered by conceptual thinking and live the real reality.
I think I blew it.
I had another little bit more from Uchiyama that was just getting started.
I think I'm missing a page, and I didn't bring the book, so that's okay, we'll let it go for next time.
He goes on to talk about moving beyond moving through abstract concepts, going deeper, going through, letting go, and that is what Dogen has been talking about here.
So we got him in there too.
Anyone have any thoughts or comments or appreciations for Dogen and Suzuki Roshi and Uchiyama and Norman and whoever this guy is?
**Participant:** Our life.
I was just thinking about how so much of this is a process of unlearning, right?
We start to grow and we're taught that we really need to wrap ourselves around these concepts, to conceptualize, to have more advanced thought, right?
And to be more advanced, it's better than being a naive child or something.
Yeah, many of the actual skills we're taught as students evolve from conceptualizing, developing conceptual thinking.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Right, right.
Which again, they're kind of holding opposites.
Like, that's good, that's good, but sure, can we do that without completely losing contact with the real reality that's beyond concepts?
Yeah.
Actually, I thought of a poem that says this really well.
Does anyone have anything else to say, or shall I read this poem?
Oh yeah, okay, let's read this poem.
You might well have heard this poem.
It's a classic poem about this engagement with the real reality.
I almost have it memorized.
Let's see if I can get it on my gadget.
If I can't, I'll try memory.
It's Mary Oliver, "The Summer Day."
Anyone know that poem?
Here, instead of a strawberry, it's a grasshopper.
But somehow Mary Oliver, she was a really deep practitioner of poetry.
He is a deep practitioner of poetry.
*Mary Oliver, "The Summer Day."
Who made the world?
Who made the swan, and the black bear?
Who made the grasshopper?

This grasshopper, I mean, the one who has flung herself out of the grass, the one who is eating sugar out of my hand, who is moving her jaws back and forth instead of up and down, who is gazing around with her enormous and complicated eyes.
Now she lifts her pale forearms and thoroughly washes her face.
Now she snaps her wings open, and floats away.
I don't know exactly what a prayer is.
I do know how to pay attention, how to fall down into the grass, how to kneel down in the grass, how to be idle and blessed, how to stroll through the fields, which is what I've been doing all day.
Tell me, what else should I have done?
Doesn't everything die at last, and too soon?
Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?*
Beautiful, huh?
Well, yeah.
Not just any grasshopper, not just a grasshopper, a word, a concept, but this grasshopper.
This life, this wild and precious life.
She's a little rebellious in there too, like, "What else should I have done today?
Is anything more important than this?"
Okay.
